name: Fer Í

attributes.attribute: Irish hero who may once have been a god
harper whose music moved every listener
father of the twin fairy queens of Munster
lake whose springs were frozen by his music
a sleep air played on a three-stringed harp

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text:
Fer Í, also written Fer Fi, is an Irish hero who may once have been a god. A harper of Munster,
his music ruled the mood of any hall. A sad air brought weeping, a gay one brought laugher, and a quiet
strain drowsed every hearer to sleep. His tune once roused a quarrel between the two siblings raised
together, Lugaidh mac Conn and Eógan, who heard him in the open air and fell to arguing over whose home
should claim him; that fight blackened into a feud that closed with Eógan dead. The hero later fathered
Munster's two fairy queens, Aine and her twin from the same womb, Grain, a sign that sits him among the
fairy kings or a god that faded. Around Lough Gur in County Limerick lore gives him a red-haired dwarf
face and names him the brother of Aine. His suantraighe, the sleep strain, played on a harp of three
strings, hushed the earth last: the springs beside Lough Gur froze and gleamed below ice like pale
stones. Its companion pitch, gentraigh, dapples of glad notes, brought every ear to bubbling laugh again.

okr.objective: Fer I is a hero of Munster whose music could calm or gladden a world.
key_results: His sad airs made people weep and his lullabies sent them to sleep.
He was the father of the twin fairy queens Aine and Grain.
Around Lough Gur he was told as a red-haired dwarf.
His gentraighe air made all who heard it laugh with delight.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
